PostgreSQL

Source: vignettes/postgres.Rmd
postgres.Rmd

PostgreSQL is an open-source SQL database. You can use it as the data source for a Shiny app while letting the database decide what each visitor can read. For example, a row policy can restrict the same query to a different set of rows for each person.

oauth_db_postgres() opens a connection with the visitor’s access token and database role. You can then query through DBI or dbplyr. This guide uses PostgreSQL’s native OAuth support; the PostgREST guide shows an HTTP alternative that doesn’t need a local PostgreSQL driver.

Try it locally

Start Docker with Linux containers, then run this in R:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("postgres")

Open http://localhost:18100 once the launcher says it is ready. Sign in as alice / alice or bob / bob. The same query returns only that person’s rows. Click Stop demo or interrupt R to remove the containers and data.

Docker supplies PostgreSQL 18, Keycloak sign-in and the required native libraries. See Getting started for first-build requirements and certificate prompts, or ?oauth_db_demo for editing the app.

Connect your own database

Native OAuth needs PostgreSQL 18 with a token-validation module. Running this app in local R also requires Linux and a shared libpq 18 used by both RPostgres and shinyOAuthDB; build instructions follow the app. On Windows or macOS, use the Docker demo or PostgREST. Azure’s Microsoft sign-in has its own Azure PostgreSQL guide.

App value Where to get it
host, port, dbname Your database administrator or existing PostgreSQL connection settings
Issuer The identity provider’s realm or tenant OpenID configuration
Client ID and secret A registration for your Shiny app; see OAuth setup
Scope The database’s OAuth rule and the matching scope in the identity provider
Username claim The profile field that matches the database’s identity-to-role mapping
sslrootcert The CA certificate that signed the database’s TLS certificate

The next app assumes these values are ready. The server configuration and native R runtime instructions follow it.

A complete app

Create a shinyOAuth client for your own issuer. Request profile and configure the provider to include preferred_username in the validated ID token. This example assumes that username matches the PostgreSQL role provisioned for that person, as in the local demo. Set OAUTHDB_POSTGRES_ISSUER, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID, and OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET before running the app.

After signing in, click Load rows. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

pkgs <- c("shiny", "shinyOAuth", "shinyOAuthDB", "mirai", "RPostgres")
for (pkg in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

issuer <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_POSTGRES_ISSUER")

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(issuer, id_token_validation = TRUE)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "database.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())
  con <- oauth_db_postgres(
    auth$connection,
    host = "postgres.example.org",
    dbname = "reporting",
    user = function() {
      reference <- req(auth$connection())
      identity <- reference$identity(claims = "preferred_username")
      req(identity$id_token_claims$preferred_username)
    },
    issuer = issuer,
    scope = "database.read",
    sslrootcert = "path/to/ca.pem"
  )
  query_task <- oauth_db_task(con)
  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke("SELECT current_user AS database_user")
  })
  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)
    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.

user is the database role requested when opening a PostgreSQL connection. The callback derives it from the currently signed-in account’s validated identity, so signing in as a different person changes the requested role. PostgreSQL checks that the access token is allowed to use that role and applies its grants and row policies.

If your database roles differ from the provider’s usernames, adapt the callback to the server’s mapping. Use a fixed user only when the database intentionally maps the permitted identities to a shared role.

Prepare PostgreSQL and the identity provider

PostgreSQL’s native OAuth needs an installed token-validation module. The example uses Percona’s pg_oidc_validator, pinned and patched to validate the database audience. Copy the demo files with oauth_db_demo(action = "files"); postgres/Dockerfile and postgres/patches/validator-audience.patch show the build.

Register a Web OAuth client in Keycloak with your Shiny callback URL, authorization code flow and PKCE. Configure the database access token’s audience and the database.read scope. The demo’s realm.json provides a complete example, including demo subjects, audience mappers and scopes.

Configure PostgreSQL’s validator to check token signatures, issuer, expiry, audience and the required scope. Map the validated subject to a database role. A corresponding pg_hba.conf rule looks like:

hostssl reporting alice,bob 10.0.0.0/24 oauth issuer="https://login.example.org/realms/reporting" scope="database.read" validator=pg_oidc_validator map=keycloak_subjects

In pg_ident.conf, map each user’s Keycloak ID (sub) to a database role:

keycloak_subjects 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111 alice
keycloak_subjects 22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222 bob

Those IDs belong to the demo accounts; use your users’ real IDs. Create the roles, grant database access, and configure table grants and row policies. The installed demo contains complete files under postgres/config/ and SQL under postgres/sql/01-fixture.sql.

Build the native R runtime

The current native adapter supports Linux with libpq major version 18. Both RPostgres and shinyOAuthDB must link the same shared libpq instance. Build libpq with --without-libcurl and leave the optional libpq-oauth device-flow module uninstalled. shinyOAuth obtains tokens through browser sign-in; a retained broken database handle must not start another login.

For a custom Linux image, install libpq’s development files and pkg-config, point PKG_CONFIG_PATH and the dynamic library search path at that libpq, then build RPostgres and shinyOAuthDB from source:

install.packages("RPostgres", type = "source")
Sys.setenv(SHINYOAUTHDB_POSTGRES_OAUTH = "required")
install.packages("shinyOAuthDB", type = "source")

These source installs rebuild the packages against the selected libpq. Setting SHINYOAUTHDB_POSTGRES_OAUTH to required makes installation fail if the native adapter cannot be built. The default, auto, builds it when the required Linux/libpq 18 development files are available. disabled builds the other backends without this adapter. Windows and macOS can use oauth_db_demo("postgres").

Connection lifetime

Call con() before every operation. A valid connection survives ordinary token refresh. Sign-out, permission loss, account changes and Shiny session end close it. After a connection failure, obtain a new handle through con(); resetting or cloning a retained native handle is unsupported. Use separate R processes for separate workers.

PostgreSQL documents OAuth authentication and validator modules.
